title: Host waits on the device inside every step
score_basis: half the measured sync share (time inside a sync includes device work that still has to run)
evidence: 2.0 blocking reads of mps tensors per step (.item(), .cpu(), .tolist(), float(), bool() or synchronize()), 6.5 ms per step blocked in them (37% of step time).
suggestion: Keep running metrics on the device (for example running_loss += loss.detach()) and read them with .item() only when you log, every N steps. Avoid float(t), bool(t), .cpu() and printing tensors inside the step.
expected_effect: Lets the host queue step N+1 while the device still runs step N. The gain is at most the host-side time per step that is currently serialized; large on small models, small on big ones.
risk_note: Training math is unchanged; you log less often.

title: No mixed precision on hardware that supports it
score_basis: 0.1 x compute ('other') share of step time
evidence: Device mps, this torch build supports autocast on MPS; autocast was never entered and parameters are float32. 57% of step time is compute and Python ('other').
suggestion: Wrap the forward pass and loss in `with torch.autocast('mps', dtype=torch.float16):`. Gains on Apple GPUs vary by op, so measure.
expected_effect: Largest on compute-bound models dominated by matmuls and convolutions; little or none when data loading or sync dominates.
risk_note: Lower precision changes numerics. bf16 rarely needs loss scaling; fp16 needs GradScaler. Check the loss trajectory with compare.

title: Logging on every step
score_basis: measured stdout/stderr write share (floor 0.02 when logging every step)
evidence: 1.0 lines written to stdout/stderr per step, 0% of step time spent writing them. Printing a metric usually needs .item(), which also forces a device sync.
suggestion: Log every N steps (for example every 50) and aggregate metrics on the device in between.
expected_effect: Small by itself; larger when each log line also forces a device sync.

title: torch.compile is not used
score_basis: prior 0.03 for mps x compute ('other') share
evidence: torch 2.14.1 supports torch.compile and it was never called. 57% of step time is compute and Python overhead, which is what compilation reduces.
suggestion: Try `model = torch.compile(model)`. Support for MPS is newer than for CUDA and CPU; expect some models to fall back or run slower. Compare with more warmup steps (for example --warmup-steps 20): compilation happens in the first steps.
expected_effect: Fewer kernel launches and less Python overhead per step. Compilation adds startup time, so it pays off on long runs.
risk_note: Same math in principle, but fused kernels can differ in the last bits, and graph breaks or recompiles can make a run slower. Measure.
